title: Reading Food Labels
summary: How to read the serving size, nutrients, ingredients, allergy warnings, and dates on a food label to make healthier choices.
poll: The pictures on the front of a food package tell you enough to choose a healthy snack.

versions.title: Read the Label
versions.text:
Pick up a box of food. Turn it to the back. You will see a label. It tells what is in the food. Let's read it!

The front may have fun art. It may have big words. But the back has the facts. In Saudi Arabia, the label is in Arabic.

First, look at the serving. A serving is one part. A bag may hold two. Eat the whole bag? Then you eat two servings.

Next, look at sugar and salt. Too much is bad for you. Eat just a bit.

Then read the ingredients. It is a list. It shows what is in the food. The first thing is the most. Is sugar first? Then it has lots of sugar.

Nuts make some kids sick. So can milk. The label tells them. Then they know.

The label has a date, too. Do not eat old food.

Look at two snacks. Which has less sugar? Pick that one. It is the healthy one!

The label has a date, too. Do not eat food when it is too old.

Now look at two snacks side by side. Which one has less sugar? That is the healthy one to pick!

versions.title: What Is on the Label?
versions.text:
Pick up a box of food and turn it over. On the back or side, you will find a label. The label tells you what is inside the food you eat.

The front of the box may have bright pictures and big words like "natural." Do not be fooled. The back is where the real facts are. In Saudi Arabia, food labels must be in Arabic. Many also have English.

First, look at the serving size. A serving is the amount the facts on the label are for. A bag of chips may hold two servings. Eat the whole bag, and you eat twice as much.

Next, check the sugar and salt. Your body needs a little, but too much is not good for your heart and teeth.

Then read the ingredients. This is a list of everything in the food. The item there is the most of comes first. If sugar is near the top of the list, the food has a lot of sugar.

Some people get very sick from foods like nuts or milk. The label warns them if these foods are inside.

The label also shows a date. It tells you when the food is no longer best to eat.

Now look at two snacks side by side. Which one has less sugar and salt? You can choose the healthy one!

versions.title: What Is on the Label?
versions.text:
Pick up a box of food from your kitchen and turn it over. On the back or side, you will find a label. This label tells you what is inside the food you are about to eat.

The front of the box may have bright pictures and big words like "natural" or "healthy." The back, though, is where the real facts are. In Saudi Arabia, food labels must be written in Arabic, and many also include English.

First, look at the serving size. A serving is the amount that all the numbers on the label describe. A bag of chips may hold two servings. If you eat the whole bag, you eat twice the sugar and salt shown.

Next, check the sugar and salt. Your body needs a small amount of each. However, eating too much over many years can harm your heart and teeth.

Then read the ingredients. This is a list of everything in the food. The item that the food has the most of always comes first. So if sugar is near the top, the food contains a lot of sugar.

Some people get very sick from foods such as nuts or milk. The label warns them when these foods are inside.

The label also shows a date that tells you when the food is no longer best to eat.

Finally, compare two snacks side by side. Which one has less sugar and salt? Now you can make a healthy choice!

versions.title: Reading Food Labels
versions.text:
Pick up any box of food in your kitchen and turn it over. Somewhere on the back or side, you will find a label. This label tells you what is inside the food you are about to eat.

The front of a package often shows bright pictures and big words like "natural." The back, however, is where the real facts are. In Saudi Arabia, food labels must be written in Arabic, and many include English, too.

Start with the serving size. All the numbers on the label describe one serving. A bag of chips may contain two servings, so eating the whole bag means eating twice the amounts listed.

Next, look at the calories. Calories measure the energy that food gives your body. Then check the nutrients, such as sugar, fat, protein, and fiber. Salt is often listed as sodium. Your body needs some of these, but too much sugar or sodium over many years can harm your heart and teeth.

Then read the ingredients list. Ingredients are always listed from the largest amount to the smallest. If sugar appears near the top, the food contains a lot of it.

Some people have an allergy to foods like nuts or milk, which can make them very sick. Labels warn them when these foods are inside.

Labels also show a date. It tells you when the food is no longer at its best or safe to eat.

Finally, compare two snacks side by side. The one with less sugar and sodium is usually the healthier choice.

versions.title: How to Read a Food Label
versions.text:
Pick up almost any package of food in your kitchen and turn it over. Somewhere on the back or side, you will discover a label that explains exactly what is inside the food you are about to eat.

The front of a package often displays colorful pictures and catchy words like "natural," which are designed to attract shoppers. The back, however, is where the real facts are printed. In Saudi Arabia, food labels must be written in Arabic, and many include English as well.

Begin with the serving size, because every number on the label describes a single serving. A bag of chips may contain two servings, so eating the entire bag means consuming twice the amounts listed.

Next, examine the calories, which measure the energy that food provides to your body. Then check the nutrients, including sugar, fat, protein, and fiber. Salt is usually listed as sodium. Your body requires some of these nutrients, but consuming too much sugar or sodium over many years can damage your heart and teeth.

After that, read the ingredients list carefully. Ingredients are always listed in order from the largest amount to the smallest, so if sugar appears near the top, the food contains a great deal of it.

Sugar can also hide under other names, such as syrup or words ending in "ose," like glucose.

Some people have an allergy to foods such as nuts or milk, which can make them seriously ill. Labels warn these shoppers whenever such foods are included.

Labels also display a date, which tells you when the food will no longer be at its best or safe to eat.

Finally, compare two similar snacks side by side. The one with less sugar and sodium is usually the healthier choice.

versions.title: Reading Food Labels
versions.text:
Pick up almost any package of food in your kitchen and turn it over, and somewhere on the back or side you will discover a label that explains precisely what is inside the food you are about to eat, and learning to read it is a skill that can protect your health for the rest of your life.

The front of a package frequently displays colorful pictures and appealing words like "natural," which manufacturers design to attract shoppers but which can sometimes be misleading. The back, however, is where the genuine facts are printed, and in Saudi Arabia these labels must be written in Arabic, although many include English as well.

Begin with the serving size, because every number on the label describes a single serving. A bag of chips might contain two servings, so a person who eats the entire bag will consume twice the amounts listed.

Next, examine the calories, which measure the energy that food provides to your body. Then check the nutrients, including sugar, fat, protein, and fiber. Salt is typically listed as sodium. Your body requires a certain amount of these nutrients, but regularly consuming excessive sugar or sodium over many years can damage your heart and teeth, so the wisest approach is moderation.

After that, read the ingredients list carefully. Ingredients are always arranged in descending order by weight, from the largest quantity to the smallest, so if sugar appears near the top, the food contains a considerable amount of it.

Be aware that sugar frequently hides under other names, such as syrup, honey, or chemical terms ending in "ose," like glucose and fructose, so a product may contain several types of sugar even when the word itself never appears.

Some people have an allergy to foods such as nuts or milk, which can make them seriously ill. Labels therefore highlight each allergen whenever such foods are included.

Labels also display an expiry date, which indicates when the food will no longer be at its best or safe to consume.

Finally, compare two similar snacks side by side. The product with less sugar and sodium is usually the healthier choice.

versions.title: Decoding the Food Label
versions.text:
Pick up almost any package of food in your kitchen and turn it over, and somewhere on the back or side you will discover a label that explains precisely what is inside the food you are about to eat, and learning to interpret it is an invaluable skill that can safeguard your health throughout your life.

The front of a package frequently displays colorful illustrations and appealing descriptions like "natural," which manufacturers deliberately design to attract shoppers but which can occasionally be misleading. The back, however, is where the genuine facts are printed. In Saudi Arabia, food labels must be written in Arabic, and numerous products include English translations as well.

Be aware that sugar frequently hides under alternative names, such as syrup, honey, or chemical terminology ending in "ose," like glucose and fructose, so a single product may contain several varieties of sugar even when the word itself never appears, which means the combined quantity can be considerably larger than shoppers anticipate.

versions.title: Decoding the Food Label
versions.text:
Learning to interpret a food label properly is one of the most practical skills a person can develop, since the information printed there, rather than the colorful marketing on the front of the package, reveals what is genuinely inside the food a person is about to consume. In Saudi Arabia, food labels must be printed in Arabic, though numerous products additionally include English translations for international shoppers.

The front of most packages displays attractive illustrations alongside persuasive descriptions such as natural, phrases that manufacturers deliberately design to attract shoppers' attention but that can occasionally prove misleading, since such claims are not independently verified facts but marketing language chosen specifically to sell the product. The genuine nutritional facts are instead printed on the back or side of the package, where a careful reader can find what truly matters.

Every number appearing on a food label describes a single serving, a detail easily overlooked. A bag of chips, for example, might contain two full servings rather than one, meaning that a person who eats the entire bag actually consumes twice the quantities listed on the label, including twice the calories, sugar, and sodium.

Beyond serving size, shoppers should examine the calories, which measure the energy a food provides to the body, alongside key nutrients such as sugar, fat, protein, and fiber, with salt typically listed under its scientific name, sodium. The body genuinely needs moderate amounts of these nutrients, but consistently consuming excessive sugar or sodium over many years can seriously damage the heart and teeth, which explains why nutrition experts consistently recommend moderation rather than total avoidance.

The ingredients list deserves particularly careful attention, since ingredients are always arranged in descending order by weight, from the largest quantity present down to the smallest. If sugar appears near the very beginning of this list, the product almost certainly contains a substantial amount of it. Complicating matters further, sugar frequently hides under alternative names such as syrup, honey, or chemical terms ending in ose, including glucose and fructose, meaning a single product may contain several different varieties of sugar even when the word sugar itself never explicitly appears anywhere on the label.

Food labels additionally serve a critical safety function for people with allergies, since any allergen present, such as nuts or milk, must be clearly highlighted, protecting those who could become dangerously ill from accidental exposure. Finally, every label displays an expiry date indicating when the food will no longer retain its best quality or remain safe to eat, making the comparison of two similar snacks side by side, choosing whichever contains less sugar and sodium overall, a genuinely healthier and more informed choice.

versions.title: Decoding the Food Label
versions.text:

The front of most commercial packages displays attractive illustrations alongside persuasive descriptive language such as natural, phrases that manufacturers deliberately and strategically design to attract shoppers' immediate attention but that can occasionally prove genuinely misleading, since such promotional claims are not independently verified scientific facts but rather marketing language carefully chosen specifically to sell the product more effectively. The genuine nutritional facts are instead printed on the back or side of the package, where a sufficiently careful reader can locate what actually matters nutritionally.

Every single number appearing anywhere on a food label describes precisely one serving, a frequently overlooked detail with significant consequences. A bag of chips, for example, might contain two complete servings rather than merely one, meaning that a person who consumes the entire bag actually ends up eating twice the quantities explicitly listed on the label, including twice the calories, sugar, and sodium originally stated.

Beyond simple serving size, careful shoppers should additionally examine the calories, which measure the energy a given food provides to the human body, alongside key nutrients such as sugar, fat, protein, and fiber, with salt typically listed under its precise scientific name, sodium. The human body genuinely requires moderate amounts of these various nutrients, but consistently consuming excessive sugar or sodium over the course of many years can seriously and progressively damage the heart and teeth, which explains why nutrition experts consistently and emphatically recommend moderation rather than complete avoidance of these substances.

The ingredients list deserves particularly careful and sustained attention, since ingredients are invariably arranged in strict descending order by weight, proceeding from the largest quantity present down systematically to the smallest. If sugar appears near the very beginning of this ordered list, the product almost certainly contains a substantial quantity of it. Complicating matters considerably further, sugar frequently conceals itself under alternative names such as syrup, honey, or chemical terminology ending in ose, including glucose and fructose, meaning that a single product may contain several entirely different varieties of sugar even when the specific word sugar itself never explicitly appears anywhere on the printed label.

Food labels additionally serve a critical, potentially life-saving safety function for individuals with allergies, since any allergen present, such as nuts or milk, must be clearly and conspicuously highlighted, protecting those who could otherwise become dangerously ill following accidental exposure. Finally, every properly printed label displays an expiry date indicating precisely when the food will no longer retain its optimal quality or remain safe to eat, making the deliberate comparison of two broadly similar snacks side by side, ultimately choosing whichever option contains less sugar and sodium overall, a genuinely healthier and considerably more informed consumer choice.

wrong.A: There is no story or characters.
wrong.B: The article does not name the best snacks.
wrong.D: No shoppers debate in the article.

MID.prompt: Your friend wants to choose a healthier snack. Write directions that tell how to use a food label. Use the words calories and sodium.
checklist: I gave clear steps in order.
I used the words calories and sodium correctly.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
MID.modelAnswer: First, check the serving size so you know what all the numbers on the label describe. Next, look at the calories, which measure the energy the food gives your body, and check nutrients like sugar and sodium, since too much of either over time can harm your heart. Finally, compare two snacks side by side, and choose the one with less sugar and sodium for the healthier choice.

keyWords.definition: giving the wrong idea, even if it is not exactly false
keyWords.example: The sign was misleading, because the shop was closed that day.

keyWords.definition: having a reasonable amount, not too much
keyWords.example: Sweets are fine in moderation, such as on special days.

keyWords.definition: going from the highest or largest to the lowest or smallest
keyWords.example: The teacher read the scores in descending order, from highest to lowest.

keyWords.definition: something, like a food, that can cause an allergy
keyWords.example: Peanuts are a common allergen in many schools.
Athletes consume more water on hot days.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the central idea of the article?
options: Understanding each part of a label helps people eat more healthily.
Food companies are not allowed to put any pictures on their packages.
Sugar should be removed completely from all foods.
Expiry dates are the only important part of a label.
questions.why: The article explains serving size, nutrients, ingredients, allergens, and dates, showing how each helps a shopper choose wisely.

wrong.B: The article describes pictures on packages; it does not say they are banned.
wrong.C: The article recommends moderation, not removing sugar entirely.
wrong.D: The date is only one of many parts the article explains.

questions.stem: How are ingredients arranged on a food label?
options: In alphabetical order
From the healthiest to the least healthy
In descending order by weight
In the order they were added during cooking
questions.why: The article says ingredients are arranged in descending order by weight, from largest to smallest.

wrong.A: The article does not mention alphabetical order.
wrong.B: The order is based on weight, not health.
wrong.D: The article does not mention cooking order.

questions.stem: Which of these is a name sugar may hide under, according to the article?
options: Sodium
Glucose
Protein
Fiber
questions.why: The article lists glucose and fructose as names ending in "ose" that mean sugar.

wrong.A: Sodium is the name for salt.

questions.stem: Why might a product contain more sugar than a shopper expects?
options: The serving size is always the whole package.
Sugar is never listed on the label.
Labels in Arabic do not show sugar.
Sugar may appear under several different names.
questions.why: The article explains that sugar hides under names like syrup, honey, and glucose, so the total can be larger than expected.

wrong.A: The article says a package can hold more than one serving.
wrong.B: Sugar is listed, sometimes under other names.
wrong.C: The language of the label does not hide sugar.

questions.stem: What can you infer about words like "natural" on the front of a package?
options: They help sell the product but do not prove it is healthy.
They are checked facts that guarantee the food is healthy.
They tell you exactly how many calories the food has.
They are required by law on every food package.
questions.why: The article says manufacturers design these words to attract shoppers and that they can be misleading, so they are not proof.

wrong.B: The article warns that these words can mislead.
wrong.C: Calories are listed on the back, not in these words.
wrong.D: The article does not say these words are required.

questions.stem: A label shows 150 calories per serving and 3 servings per package. How many calories would you consume by eating the whole package?
questions.why: Every number describes one serving, so three servings mean 3 × 150 = 450 calories.

wrong.D: This adds the numbers instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: "nutrition experts consistently recommend moderation." What does moderation mean?
options: Eating only one kind of food
Eating reasonable amounts, not too much
Never eating sugar or salt
Eating as much as you want
questions.why: The body needs some sugar and sodium, but too much is harmful, so moderation means a reasonable amount.

wrong.A: The article does not suggest eating one kind of food.
wrong.C: The article says the body needs some of these nutrients.
wrong.D: Eating as much as you want is the opposite of moderation.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by asking readers to pick up a package and turn it over?
options: To explain how packages are made
To show that most packages are empty
To list the foods found in a kitchen
To connect the topic to something readers can do right away
questions.why: The opening invites readers to take part, which makes the skill of reading a label feel real and useful.

wrong.A: The article does not explain how packages are made.
wrong.B: Nothing in the article says packages are empty.
wrong.C: The article does not list kitchen foods.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say the front of a package is enough to judge a food. Do you agree? Explain your answer using at least three details from the article.
checklist: I clearly stated whether I agree or disagree.
I used at least three details from the article.
I organized my answer in clear, complete sentences.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that the front of a package is enough to judge a food, because the article shows the front can be misleading with bright pictures and words like "natural" that do not tell you the real facts. The back of the label lists ingredients in descending order from largest to smallest amount, so if sugar is near the top, you are about to consume a lot of it, which the front never shows. The label also warns about allergens like nuts or milk and reminds shoppers to eat certain foods only in moderation, information that a pretty front picture simply cannot provide.
